## Before you begin

No prior R or GLM experience is required. The instructor will explain the example.
You may run the supplied code and change only the two counts, or use
[the two-survey result sheet](results.html) to compare the prepared figures.
Both routes complete the same exercise: predict, compare uncertainty, and explain
what you see. Allow **12 minutes**, including discussion. No installation,
independent programming or homework is required. For optional local code execution,
see [packages and setup](../classroom/PACKAGES.md).

```{r participant-setup}
library(tidyverse)
theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 14))
```

# Core exercise: more seedlings, how much uncertainty?

The code below is a starting example: 2 survivors out of 5 seedlings.

```{r core-data-comparison, fig.height=3.4}
y <- 2
N <- 5
p <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 101)

prior <- dbeta(p, shape1 = 1, shape2 = 1) # flat prior
likelihood <- dbinom(x = y, size = N, prob = p) # likelihood
posterior <- prior * likelihood
posterior <- posterior / sum(posterior) # weights sum to 1

tibble(p = p, posterior = posterior) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = p, y = posterior)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, colour = "#d95f02") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    x = "Survival probability p",
    y = "Posterior probability per grid point",
    title = paste(y, "survivors out of", N, "seedlings")
  )
```

1. Choose a small survey and a larger survey, both with an observed survival proportion of 0.4. Write down the number surveyed (`N`) and the number surviving (`y`) for each.
2. Before running the code, predict which survey will give a narrower posterior.
3. If running R, use your counts in the code above. Copy the code into a new chunk for the second survey so that both plots remain visible. Keep the prior and grid unchanged.
   If reading the result sheet, use its prepared 4/10 and 20/50 surveys instead.
4. Compare the two plots. Does the result agree with your prediction? Explain what the curve widths tell you about uncertainty in the survival probability.
